limitations: This record does not assess whether model providers changed their prices after October 2025.

That is $4.585 billion, which rounds to $4.6 billion.
limitations: Zitron's source was a Reuters report on a leaked draft. The record checks his figure against the S-1 as filed.

our_interpretation: We read 'endlessly hyped' as leading AI companies promoting agents at points spread across 2025, including its last quarter.

criteria.support_condition: Leading AI companies promoted agents at points spread across 2025, including its last quarter, and independent tests published late in 2025 show general-purpose agents failing a large share of realistic multi-step work tasks.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Independent tests published late in 2025 show general-purpose agents completing most realistic multi-step work tasks across broad uses, or agents were not prominently promoted during 2025.

payload.rationale: On January 1, 2025, under 'High confidence', Marcus predicted that AI agents would be endlessly hyped throughout 2025 but far from reliable, except possibly in very narrow use cases. OpenAI promoted agents in January, June, and October 2025, from saying they may 'join the workforce' to launching tools to build them. Independent benchmarks found the best agent completed 30% of simulated workplace tasks (September 2025) and 2.5% of real remote-work projects (30 October 2025).
limitations: The promotion shown comes from one company, OpenAI. It does not measure how much agents were promoted across the industry.
Both benchmarks are preprints, and the latest is from 30 October 2025, not the end of the year.
Whether an agent use counts as a 'very narrow use case' is not defined by the speaker.

payload.rationale: The claim has two parts, and the contract requires support for both. The first part is that no LLM is fully coherent. The second part is that the cause is repeating conflicting training data instead of reasoning. No study in the evidence tests this cause. Rozado's February 2024 preprint gives preliminary evidence that political preferences may be embedded mostly after pretraining, during fine-tuning or reinforcement learning (e2). The author calls this not conclusive. It is about where political preferences come from, not about coherence. from_speaker: But is getting enough better? (rhetorical question, not an assertion)
our_interpretation: Only the first sentence is a checkable assertion: that Tesla's Full Self-Driving software was improving at the time of the post. The second sentence is a question, so it is not graded.
He named no period. I read 'is getting better' as recent progress in the months before the 2024-04-09 post, which in practice means the FSD v12 rollout from January to early April 2024.
Plain reading: crowdsourced or reported performance data, such as miles between disengagements, or broad reports on driving quality show the newer FSD versions doing better than earlier ones.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence from early 2024 shows newer FSD versions, such as v12.x, performing better than earlier versions, for example more miles between critical disengagements or clearly better reported driving.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence from early 2024 shows FSD performance flat or getting worse compared with earlier versions.

payload.rationale: Marcus wrote that Tesla FSD 'is getting better' and then asked whether it was getting enough better. Under the contract, only the first sentence is graded. The second is a question. A March 18, 2024 report (e2) said Tesla had widely released FSD v12.3 in the US, using end-to-end neural nets. It said owners commonly described the car's movements as much smoother and more human-like, and said it made correct decisions it never could before. An April 2, 2024 summary of crowdsourced FSD tracker data (e1) reported 448 miles between critical disengagements for v12.3. The summary said this was over three times the best v11 result and over four times any v10 result. Both items are dated before the April 9, 2024 post, and both describe newer versions doing better than earlier ones. That meets the contract's support condition. The packet contains no counterevidence.
limitations: The tracker figures in e1 come from crowdsourced, self-reported data. e1 notes that data for later v12.3.x releases still needed weeks to be entered.
e2's account of driving quality summarizes owner feedback and social media posts, not a controlled test.
The evidence contains no official Tesla intervention or disengagement data and no independent hands-on review from the period.
The evidence does not show whether the improvement was enough for unsupervised or robotaxi operation. The 'enough better' question is not graded.

evidence.excerpt: They are now recording 448 Miles between critical disengagements for Tesla FSD 12.3 Supervised. This is over three times better than the best results for any Tesla FSD v11.X
evidence.explanation: Crowdsourced tracker data as of early April 2024 showed v12.3 with far more miles between critical disengagements than v11 or v10, a measurable improvement just before the post.

evidence.excerpt: The common thread in the feedback from owners about v12.3 is that car’s movements are much smoother and feels more human-like, and that it can make correct decisions in the heat of the moment that it never could before.
evidence.explanation: A contemporaneous report on the v12.3 wide release says owners widely saw better driving than in earlier versions.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: a meaningful part of the human filtering work for ChatGPT was done by Kenyan workers who took home under about $2 per hour and labelled graphic text, including child sexual abuse and bestiality.
Period: the Sama text-labelling contract for OpenAI, from November 2021 to March 2022.
'Less than $2/hour' is read as take-home pay up to about $2, matching the TIME headline he cites.
criteria.support_condition: Reliable reporting shows Kenyan contractors labelled graphic sexual content involving children and animals for OpenAI's ChatGPT safety work, for take-home pay of about $2/hour or less.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable evidence shows the workers were paid well above $2/hour, did not label such material, or that the work was unrelated to ChatGPT.

payload.rationale: TIME published its report on 2023-01-18. It says that, starting in November 2021, OpenAI sent tens of thousands of text snippets to an outsourcing firm in Kenya to get them labelled. Some of those snippets described child sexual abuse and bestiality in graphic detail (e2). TIME reviewed internal Sama and OpenAI documents, including payslips, and interviewed four Sama employees who worked on the project. It reports that the labellers Sama employed for OpenAI took home about $1.32 to $2 per hour, depending on seniority and performance (e1). So the top of that range is $2, and the rest is below it. A Sama spokesperson said workers could earn $1.46 to $3.74 per hour after taxes (e3). The pay and tasks TIME reports match the claim that a bunch of the work was done by Kenyan workers paid under $2 per hour to label this kind of material.
limitations: All the evidence comes from one investigative report, TIME's article of 2023-01-18. No independent source in the packet confirms the pay figures or what the tasks involved.
The quoted passages describe labelling work done for OpenAI. They do not by themselves spell out how that work fed into ChatGPT.
TIME's range goes up to about $2 per hour, which is not strictly less than $2.
Sama gave a higher range of $1.46 to $3.74 per hour, and the packet notes it was not broken down by role. It cannot be fully squared with TIME's payslip-based figures.
The evidence does not show what share of all of ChatGPT's human filtering work these Kenyan workers did.

evidence.excerpt: The data labelers employed by Sama on behalf of OpenAI were paid a take-home wage of between around $1.32 and $2 per hour depending on seniority and performance.
evidence.explanation: Based on payslips, Kenyan labellers took home about $1.32–$2 per hour, which matches 'less than $2/hour'.

evidence.excerpt: Some of it described situations in graphic detail like child sexual abuse, bestiality, murder, suicide, torture, self harm, and incest.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the Kenyan workers labelled graphic descriptions of child sexual abuse and bestiality.

evidence.excerpt: workers could earn between $1.46 and $3.74 per hour after taxes.

our_interpretation: The comparison runs from approximately April 2022 to June 1, 2024, inferred from the post's 26-month comparison.
The ordinary reading concerns progress toward reliably keeping AI behavior aligned with human intentions, including under unfamiliar conditions and increasing capability.
Being unsolved does not establish that no progress occurred. Conversely, improving a particular safety benchmark does not by itself establish progress toward a general solution.
Research addressing specific alignment obstacles is material counterevidence, but judging the overall distance to a solution requires a link between those advances and the broader problem.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable evidence shows that the principal barriers to dependable alignment were no nearer resolution in June 2024 than around April 2022, accounting for relevant advances and their limitations.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Validated theoretical or empirical advances demonstrably remove or reduce a substantive barrier to a general alignment solution relative to the 2022 baseline.

payload.rationale: Research during the comparison period reports advances in behavioral control and supervision, so a literal claim that alignment research made no progress faces substantial counterevidence. But Marcus says no closer to a solution to the alignment problem. The sources do not establish how those advances change the distance to a general solution. The international assessment explicitly separates improved control of some systems from uncertainty about future control. Neither continuing failures nor these limited advances settle the broader comparison.
limitations: A narrower interpretation covering any improvement in present-model alignment would favor contradiction.
The original studies report results from their developers and do not establish dependable alignment across future systems.
The assessment does not equate an unsolved problem with a lack of progress.

evidence.explanation: The authors report progress in controlling assistant behavior while reducing human supervision. This challenges a literal claim of no alignment research progress, but does not demonstrate a general solution or establish its distance from completion.

The study finds that weaker supervisors can elicit some stronger-model capabilities, addressing a relevant supervision obstacle. Its experiments are an analogy to future superhuman alignment, and the authors acknowledge that naive methods fail to recover full capabilities.

evidence.publisher: International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI, published by the UK government
evidence.explanation: The assessment notes improved control in some recent systems while finding the direction of future controllability uncertain. It supports separating demonstrated local advances from an established trajectory toward a general solution.

payload.what_would_resolve: A specified alignment objective and a comparable 2022–2024 assessment showing whether validated advances reduced its principal barriers, including evidence that those advances generalize beyond the tested settings.

our_interpretation: In context, the ordinary reading is that general-purpose AI lacked dependable anticipation of the real-world consequences and harms of its recommendations.

payload.rationale: The evidence does not settle the claim at its stated breadth. AHA! shows useful generation of possible harms, and SafetyBench shows measurable safety understanding alongside errors. Neither establishes dependable prediction of real-world consequences, nor proves that contemporary AI had no reliable method. The closest studies assess related abilities rather than the claimed capability.
Specialized predictive systems could matter under a broader reading of current AI.

evidence.explanation: AHA! demonstrates that language models could help surface meaningful possible harms, qualifying any reading that denies all harm-anticipation ability. It does not measure dependable prediction of actual consequences of the model's recommendations, and predates the October window.

This is relevant counterweight to a blanket incapacity claim, but neither the measured task nor the reporting period matches the decisive test specified here.

payload.what_would_resolve: Evaluations of systems available by October 26, 2023, that directly test anticipated consequences and missed harms across realistic recommendations, with a justified reliability standard and clear coverage of available methods.

from_speaker: large language models won’t be jailbroken
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading concerns general immunity from jailbreaks in useful, general-purpose LLMs, rather than guarantees limited to a specified attack family.
Unethical things means harmful outputs that violate the tested models' safety restrictions.

Quickly and automatically means an attack-generation process requiring no human intervention during its iterations and a modest number of queries or minutes. It does not imply success on every attempt or every model.
I use October 1 through October 26, 2023, for the current research-state observation and the just-published technique.
criteria.support_condition: An October 2023 publication demonstrates automated, relatively fast jailbreaks on multiple current LLMs, while examined defense guarantees do not establish general immunity.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The cited technique does not automate successful jailbreak discovery or does not operate quickly, or a contemporary defense establishes general immunity across the relevant jailbreak threat space.

payload.rationale: PAIR directly supports the claim about quick, automated jailbreaks across multiple contemporary LLMs. Its success varied markedly by model. Erase-and-check and SmoothLLM offered restricted guarantees, so Marcus's wording would be too broad if read as denying every kind of guarantee. Under the ordinary reading of general jailbreak immunity, those defenses do not contradict the claim.
limitations: The guarantee clause depends on the stated general-immunity interpretation.
PAIR did not succeed on every model or harmful request.
The experiments test specified harmful behaviors, not every possible meaning of unethical.
The attack evidence comes from the authors' original preprint.

evidence.locator: Section 1; results in Table 1 and the discussion following Table 2
evidence.explanation: The published demonstration reports roughly five-minute successful jailbreak generation and success rates of 60% for GPT-3.5, 62% for GPT-4, and 72% for PaLM-2. Success was substantially lower for Llama-2 and Claude, so the evidence establishes capability across multiple models rather than uniform vulnerability.

Erase-and-check is material counterevidence to a literal assertion that no guarantees of any kind existed. Its protection concerns bounded modifications and a safety filter, not immunity to arbitrary jailbreaks; it also predates the selected October window.

SmoothLLM derives a high-probability defense guarantee under an assumption about how suffix attacks respond to character changes. This qualifies the sweeping wording, but does not establish general jailbreak immunity.

from_speaker: I expect the lead to be slight
with nobody retaining a sizeable a lead for long
our_interpretation: 'Lead' means the capability lead of the best US model over the best Chinese model, or the reverse, as measured by independent capability indices or leaderboards.
'Flip back and forth' means the top spot changes between US and Chinese models more than once.
No deadline is given, so the forecast is open unless a decisive multi-year record settles it.
criteria.support_condition: Over a sustained period, independent trackers show the top position alternating between US and Chinese models, with small gaps.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Over a sustained period, independent trackers show one country holding the frontier continuously with a large gap, and no flips.

payload.rationale: Marcus forecast that the US-China lead in generative AI would stay slight and flip back and forth, with no one keeping a sizeable lead for long. He gave no deadline. The only evidence is an Epoch AI data insight dated January 2, 2026 (e1). It says that since 2023 every frontier model on the Epoch Capabilities Index was developed in the US. It also says Chinese models trailed by an average of seven months, with a range of four to 14 months. So on that index the lead had not flipped by early January 2026. That record falls almost entirely before the December 13, 2025 post, and it ends a few weeks after it. The forecast concerns what happens after the post. The packet has no multi-year record after the post showing either repeated flips or an unbroken large lead, which the early-resolution rule requires. The forecast stays open.
limitations: The evidence comes from one capability index, the Epoch Capabilities Index.
The Epoch data end around January 2, 2026. The packet has no measurements from later in 2026.
'Slight', 'sizeable' and 'for long' are not quantified, and the claim names no capability measure.

evidence.excerpt: Since 2023, every model at the frontier of AI capabilities, as measured by the Epoch Capabilities Index, has been developed in the United States. Over that same period, Chinese models have trailed US capabilities by an average of seven months, with a minimum gap of four months and a maximum gap of 14.
evidence.explanation: Up to the start of 2026, the lead had not flipped on this index: the US held the frontier throughout. The gap was months, not years. This covers mostly the period before the post, so it does not settle the forecast.

payload.what_would_resolve: A multi-year independent record of top US and Chinese model capability after December 2025, such as later Epoch Capabilities Index or Arena data. Repeated changes in which country holds the top spot, with small gaps, would support the forecast. One country holding a large lead without a break would contradict it.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: generative AI models from rival providers are broadly interchangeable, so buyers choose mainly on price, and prices are pushed toward cost.
Present-tense claim: it describes the market in 2025 up to the post date.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence that models are easily swapped, that buyers choose mainly on price, and that prices for a given capability fall quickly under competition.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that buyers choose mainly on performance, pay for frontier models over cheaper equivalents, and stick with particular providers, so models are differentiated rather than interchangeable.

payload.rationale: The contract reads 'commodity' as meaning that rival models are easy to swap, that buyers choose mainly on price, and that prices for a given capability fall quickly under competition. Evidence of buyers choosing on performance, paying for frontier models and staying with one provider would contradict it. Part of the claim holds. Epoch AI (March 12, 2025) found that the price of reaching a given benchmark result fell 9x to 900x per year (e1). Menlo Ventures' mid-2025 report says switching vendors is relatively easy (e3). Part does not hold. The same report says builders 'consistently choose frontier models over cheaper, faster alternatives' and 'pay for performance' (e2). It also reports that 66% of builders upgraded within their existing provider, 23% did not switch models, and only 11% switched vendors (e3). These buyer findings match the contract's contradiction condition. The price findings match part of the support condition. The evidence does not show whether prices were pushed toward cost.
limitations: The buyer evidence comes from a single survey of builders by a venture firm, from mid-2025, months before the December 2025 post.
Epoch measured price declines at benchmark milestones. It did not measure whether buyers treat models as interchangeable, and it found no clear evidence that falling margins explain the declines.
There are no profit-margin data showing whether prices reached cost.
'Commodity' is partly a rhetorical label, so the result depends on the reading used.

evidence.excerpt: The rate of decline varies dramatically depending on the performance milestone, ranging from 9x to 900x per year.
evidence.explanation: The price of any given capability level falls very fast. That is consistent with commodity-like competition once a capability is matched.

evidence.excerpt: Performance drives decisions. Builders consistently choose frontier models over cheaper, faster alternatives.
evidence.locator: section 'Enterprises Switch Models for Performance, Not Price'
evidence.explanation: Buyers paid for top performance rather than treating models as interchangeable and choosing on price. That cuts against the commodity claim for frontier models.

evidence.excerpt:
66% of builders upgraded models within their existing provider, while 23% did not
switch models at all this past year. Only 11% switched vendors.
evidence.locator: section 'Enterprises Switch Models for Performance, Not Price'
evidence.explanation: Few buyers switched vendors. That points to provider loyalty, not commodity-style swapping, although the same report says switching is 'relatively easy.'

'Next few years' is read as roughly three to five years from December 2025. The latest plausible end is the end of 2030.

payload.rationale: Marcus forecast that over the next few years both the US and China would build a lot of generative AI infrastructure, possibly much more than they need. One year of building cannot show what happened over several years. The 'more than they need' part is hedged and can only be judged later. The forecast is not yet due.
limitations: The horizon is vague. The end date of 2030 is an interpretation.

payload.what_would_resolve: Capex filings from US and Chinese cloud and AI companies, official statistics, and data-centre capacity trackers covering roughly 2026–2028 (up to 2030). statement.excerpt: The new version is that there is not one scaling law, but three: scaling with how long you train a model (which isn’t really holding anymore), scaling with how long you post-train a model, and scaling with how long you let a given model wrestle with a given problem (or what Satya Nadella called scaling with “inference time compute”).
statement.document_title: The new AI scaling law shell game

from_speaker: scaling with how long you train a model
our_interpretation: Assess the parenthetical claim about pretraining, rather than the separate enumeration of three scaling approaches.
The plain reading is that increasing pretraining scale no longer reliably delivers the capability gains previously expected. It need not mean that every additional training step produces no benefit.
The surrounding last-few-weeks discussion places the current state in November 1–24, 2024. Older experiments provide context only.
Training duration is read in the surrounding context of pretraining compute, model size and data, rather than wall-clock time alone.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable predictions and measured frontier pretraining results for the claimed period show systematic shortfalls in expected capability gains.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable predictions and measured results for that period show that increasing pretraining scale continued reliably to deliver the expected gains.

payload.rationale: The available experimental record includes an earlier successful capability prediction for Llama 3. It does not establish what happened in the November runs Marcus discusses. Without comparable predictions and measured outcomes for that period, neither disappointing expectations nor earlier successes settle whether pretraining scaling had stopped reliably delivering expected gains.
limitations: The strongest experimental counterevidence concerns an earlier model and is context only.
Private frontier training results and their original predictions were not available in the retrieved records.
Results on one benchmark would not establish reliability across all capabilities.

evidence.excerpt: We show the results of this experiment on the ARC Challenge benchmark in Figure 4).
evidence.locator: Section 3.2, paragraph on predicting downstream performance and Figure 4
evidence.explanation: The accompanying results report an accurate extrapolation across four orders of magnitude, slightly underpredicting Llama 3's final performance. This is relevant counterevidence from an earlier model, but cannot directly settle a claim about a subsequent November breakdown.

evidence.excerpt: We investigate the optimal model size and number of tokens for training a transformer language model under a given compute budget.
evidence.explanation: The research treats training compute, model size and token count jointly. It explains why an unspecified claim about training longer needs a defined comparison, but provides no November 2024 outcome.

payload.what_would_resolve: Contemporaneous predictions and measured outcomes from multiple relevant pretraining runs, with consistent metrics and enough detail to distinguish ordinary diminishing returns from prediction failure.

our_interpretation: The target is the September 12, 2024 research disclosure identified in the claim, rather than later o1 releases or later scaling experiments.
The ordinary reading of scaling test-time compute is changing the inference budget and observing its effect on performance.
Uneven differences between o1 and GPT-4o are relevant context, but do not isolate the effect of additional inference compute.
criteria.support_condition: The cited research reports increased inference compute improving performance on some tasks while producing no improvement or worse performance on others under comparable conditions.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable task-level compute sweeps in the cited research establish improvements for all task categories covered by the alleged exceptions.

payload.rationale: The cited post reports uneven performance across tasks, but that does not establish uneven returns to extra inference compute. Its cross-model evaluations generally use o1 at maximum test-time compute. The located evidence does not settle the claim as written. Reading it simply as a claim about uneven o1-versus-GPT-4o performance would change the assessment.
limitations: The conclusion depends on distinguishing model comparisons from compute-scaling experiments.
Missing negative compute sweeps are an evidence gap, not proof that every task benefits.

evidence.excerpt: Unless otherwise specified, we evaluated o1 on the maximal test-time compute setting.
evidence.explanation: The cross-model benchmark comparisons generally use one o1 compute setting. They cannot alone show whether increasing o1's inference budget helps or fails on a particular task.

payload.what_would_resolve: Task-level data from the cited research comparing the same model at multiple inference budgets, showing both gains and non-gains.

reasons.reason: OpenAI's o1 post says performance consistently improves with more test-time compute, and no within-model sweep showing failure was found. The uneven results compare o1 with GPT-4o instead.

our_interpretation: The forecast covers both post-training and inference-time scaling.
The ordinary reading is that extending these scaling approaches will eventually cease producing meaningful performance improvements.
A plateau for one model, task or implementation is relevant but does not by itself establish that both scaling approaches have run out.
The claim supplies neither a deadline nor a numerical definition of meaningful improvement.
criteria.support_condition: Public experiments establish sustained plateaus or breakdowns in both scaling relationships across meaningful task sets as compute increases, with enough controls to distinguish the claimed limits from a particular implementation's failure.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A decisive result establishes that the claimed eventual breakdown cannot occur within the stated scope. Continued gains over a finite compute range do not refute an eventual limit.

payload.rationale: Experiments have identified real limits in particular inference and post-training methods. Other experiments have overcome apparent plateaus. These results do not decisively establish that both scaling approaches have run out. Marcus gave no deadline, so continued progress cannot make this eventual forecast false either.
limitations: A narrower reading limited to particular scaling recipes would be easier to support.
The cited limits and improvements cover finite experimental settings.

evidence.excerpt: Resampling cannot decrease this probability, so it imposes an upper bound to the accuracy of resampling-based inference scaling, regardless of compute budget.
evidence.explanation: This version reports a bound arising from imperfect verifiers. It is evidence of a specific inference-scaling limit, but does not establish limits for every inference method or for post-training.

evidence.excerpt: The divergence was clear: ProRL stagnated, while BroRL delivered steady, significant gains in less time.
evidence.explanation: The experiment reports a post-training plateau that a different rollout allocation overcame. This cautions against treating an observed plateau as exhaustion of post-training scaling generally.

payload.what_would_resolve: Reproducible compute sweeps showing sustained breakdown of both claimed scaling relationships across meaningful task sets, with controls distinguishing broad limits from implementation-specific plateaus.

our_interpretation: 'On his watch' means during Trump's current term, ending 2029-01-20.
'AI-tinged economic debacle' plainly means a major market crash, recession, or financial crisis widely linked to AI (for example, an AI bubble bursting).
'Closely tied' would be shown by mainstream reporting and polling that link the debacle to Trump and his AI or Silicon Valley policies.
criteria.support_condition: An AI-linked economic debacle occurs before 2029-01-20, and mainstream reporting and polling widely tie it to Trump and his closeness to the tech industry.
criteria.contradiction_condition: An AI-linked economic debacle occurs before 2029-01-20, but reporting and polling largely do not tie it to Trump.

payload.rationale: The claim is a conditional forecast. If an AI-linked economic debacle happens during Trump's term, he will be closely tied to it. The contract sets the window from 2025-12-12 to 2029-01-20, so the deadline has not passed. In an Anchorage Daily News report published 2026-10-25 (e1), economist Servaas Storm says there is an AI bubble in the stock market and in data center construction. He says the bubble bursting is 'not imminent, but it is approaching' and will very likely happen before Trump's presidency ends. This is one expert's forecast, not a record of a crash. The cited evidence does not show that an AI-linked crash, recession, or financial crisis has happened. It also has no polling or coverage on who would be blamed for one. The contract has no early-resolution rule. The claim cannot be scored yet.
limitations: The evidence is one news report quoting one economist. It does not measure market or economic conditions directly.
The search behind the packet was a single query. A CNN report on AI-linked market volatility from 2026-10-26 was not read in full.
The evidence has no polling or coverage on whether the public or press would tie an AI-linked debacle to Trump.
The contract sets no size threshold for 'economic debacle' and no measure of 'closely tied'.

evidence.excerpt: “That moment is not imminent, but it is approaching — and it will very likely happen before the end of Trump’s presidency.”
evidence.explanation: As of late October 2026, an economist quoted in this report describes an AI bubble that has not yet burst. That suggests the forecast's trigger has not yet happened, and the window runs to January 2029.

payload.what_would_resolve: Official economic statistics or market data showing a major AI-linked market crash, recession, or financial crisis before 2029-01-20. Then reputable polling and major news coverage showing whether it is widely tied to Trump and his closeness to the tech industry.

from_speaker: some of those completions are true

our_interpretation: Autocompletes sentences means generating text by predicting successive tokens.
Vast but finite training data is read as broad but incomplete factual coverage.
The claim attributes some correct and incorrect outputs to that coverage. It does not expressly say that data coverage is the only cause or that infinite data would guarantee truth.
The relevant systems are GPT models available when the post appeared.
criteria.support_condition: Model documentation confirms successive-token prediction, and evidence establishes that training-data coverage causally contributes to both correct answers and factual errors in the relevant GPT systems.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Documentation refutes the generation mechanism, or controlled evidence refutes the proposed contribution of training-data coverage. Other causes of errors do not alone contradict this nonexclusive claim.

payload.rationale: The autocomplete component is supported. Research also makes incomplete factual coverage a credible contributor to errors. However, the controlled coverage experiment examined another model, while the GPT-3 analysis used estimated training-data counts. Later theoretical work supplies context rather than a direct test of the relevant GPT systems. The complete causal claim therefore remains unresolved. Evidence of other error mechanisms would not, by itself, contradict his statement that coverage explains some outputs.
limitations: This assessment does not interpret finite data as the sole asserted cause.
Training-data coverage, model scale, and total data volume are different variables.
Theoretical results and experiments on other models cannot fully establish the GPT-specific attribution.

evidence.explanation: This supports the next-token prediction component. It does not establish why particular completions are true or false.

evidence.locator: Abstract, final sentence; full paper Sections 3.1–3.2 and Appendix A
evidence.explanation: The study supports a role for factual coverage, including a controlled removal experiment on a separate model. Its GPT-3 results use estimated training-data counts, so they do not directly isolate the claimed cause in GPT.

The paper explains how sparse factual support can produce errors and how evaluation incentives can preserve guessing. This supports the plausibility of a coverage mechanism without directly establishing its contribution in the GPT systems discussed in 2023.

payload.what_would_resolve: GPT-specific controlled experiments that vary relevant factual coverage while holding model size, training objectives, prompting, and evaluation constant.

reasons.reason: The GPT-4 report confirms next-token prediction. Kandpal et al. show causal links between pretraining coverage of a fact and answer accuracy, and Kalai et al. show that facts with sparse support in training data produce errors. Together these back this nonexclusive claim.

GPT-4 documentation confirms next-token prediction. Kandpal's experiments link factual coverage to accuracy, and the Nature study explains errors from sparse support, supporting the claim that incomplete coverage contributes to some false answers.

from_speaker: Each new bigger, more expensive model ekes out measurable improvements
none of these experiments has solved core issues
our_interpretation: The scored core is the firm part: that no scaled LLM had, by the post date (2025-11-27), solved hallucination, generalization, planning and reasoning. The 'returns appear to be diminishing' part is hedged ('appear') and is treated as context, not scored separately.

Plain reading of 'solved': the problem has been overcome to the point that it is no longer a basic limitation of frontier models. Steady improvement or strong results on specific benchmarks does not count as 'solved'.
Target period runs from the start of the Kaplan-laws scaling era (2020) to the post date, because the claim covers all such experiments up to then.
criteria.support_condition: Credible evidence from around late 2025 (lab research, independent evaluations, or leading researchers) showing that state-of-the-art LLMs still had substantial hallucination, generalization, planning or reasoning failures.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evidence that by late 2025 some scaled LLM had effectively eliminated one or more of these problems, for example hallucination rates near zero on open-ended factual tasks, or robust human-level generalization and planning on new tasks.

payload.rationale: Read plainly, the claim is that by late November 2025 no scaled LLM had overcome hallucination, generalization, planning and reasoning as basic limits. In September 2025, OpenAI's own researchers wrote that hallucinations 'persist even in state-of-the-art systems' (e1). In June 2025, Apple researchers found that frontier reasoning models suffer 'complete accuracy collapse' on planning puzzles past a certain complexity (e2). Two days before the post, Sutskever said models 'generalize dramatically worse than people' (e3), which confirms the post's attribution. There was real progress, such as gold-medal-level IMO results in July 2025 (e5) and what ARC Prize later called a profound upgrade in reasoning (e4). But neither source claims these problems were solved, and ARC Prize itself says reasoning systems still have many flaws. The evidence fits the claim that improvements were measurable but the core problems remained unsolved.
limitations: 'Solved' has no stated threshold. Someone who counts IMO gold or big benchmark gains as solving reasoning would read the claim differently.
The hedged diminishing-returns part was not scored.
Some evidence covers particular task families (puzzles, factual recall) rather than the four problem areas as a whole.

statement.excerpt: To a first approximation, all the big tech companies, from OpenAI to Google to Meta to xAI to Anthropic to several Chinese companies, keep doing the same experiment over and over: building ever larger LLMs in hopes of reaching AGI.

from_speaker: from OpenAI to Google to Meta to xAI to Anthropic to several Chinese companies
keep doing the same experiment over and over
our_interpretation: The plain reading is that repeatedly enlarging frontier LLMs remained a central, shared route toward AGI across the companies described. Evidence about only some named labs cannot establish the claim.

The approximation allows differences in architecture, training methods and product offerings. Smaller models and other research programs do not by themselves disprove a continuing strategy of building larger frontier LLMs.

Larger ordinarily means greater model size, established through comparable parameter counts or explicit company statements about relative size. More infrastructure, training compute, inference effort or benchmark performance alone does not establish larger models.
Total and active parameters must be distinguished when comparing mixture-of-experts models. Multimodal language models count as LLMs under this ordinary reading.

For this ongoing observation, the reporting window is the current calendar year through publication: January 1 to November 27, 2025. Earlier generations may supply comparison context. This window is an evaluator choice because the speaker supplied no starting date.
Several Chinese companies is read as at least three identifiable companies. The speaker did not identify them.
criteria.support_condition: Public records establish repeated enlargement of frontier LLMs as a central route toward AGI across major AI developers, including every named lab and at least three identifiable Chinese companies. The record must establish model enlargement and AGI intent for the same companies; infrastructure expansion or a few examples is insufficient.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Public records establish a material exception to the claimed shared strategy: a named lab, or a substantial part of the described group, was not pursuing repeated enlargement of frontier LLMs toward AGI. An isolated smaller release, additional research methods, or missing size disclosures is insufficient.

payload.rationale: OpenAI called GPT-4.5 its largest model on February 27, 2025 [e1]. Meta disclosed nearly two trillion total parameters and 288 billion active parameters for Behemoth on April 5, 2025 [e2]. Google linked Gemini 3 to AGI on November 18, 2025, as Qwen did for Qwen3 on April 29, 2025 [e3][e4]. These disclosures establish parts of the claim, but do not establish repeated enlargement toward AGI across the full group [e1][e2][e3][e4]. Google's announcement, xAI's July 9 release, and Anthropic's November 24 release provide no comparable model-size histories [e3][e5][e6]. Qwen, DeepSeek, and Baidu's records do not establish both repeated enlargement and an AGI link for all three companies [e4][e7][e8]. xAI's reinforcement learning and DeepSeek's September 29 architectural change do not establish that either company stopped pursuing larger models [e5][e7].
limitations: The evidence does not establish the complete claim for January 1 through November 27, 2025, or a material exception to it.
Missing size disclosures do not show that models did not grow.
Release announcements do not provide complete histories of private development programs.
Total parameters, active parameters, training compute, and output-token efficiency are different measures.

evidence.explanation: Directly supports enlargement for OpenAI through GPT‑4.5. It does not establish the entire cross-company claim or independently establish AGI intent.

evidence.locator: Pushing Llama to new sizes: The 2T Behemoth, first paragraph
evidence.explanation: Provides direct evidence of Meta building a very large frontier LLM, with total and active parameters distinguished. This supports a component of the claim without establishing every company's repeated enlargement or AGI intent.
Explicitly establishes AGI intent for Google's Gemini program shortly before the post. It does not establish that Gemini 3 was larger than its predecessors.
Establishes AGI intent for one Chinese company's LLM program. One such company cannot satisfy the several-companies requirement, and intention alone does not establish repeated enlargement.

Shows a substantive training development beyond enlarging a model. It cautions against treating the experiments as literally identical, but does not disprove Marcus's approximate description or establish a size trend.

evidence.locator: New on the Claude Developer Platform, discussion of effort control
evidence.explanation: Documents an efficiency improvement in Anthropic's latest pre-post model. Output-token efficiency is a different measure from model size and cannot establish either enlargement or shrinkage.
Documents an architectural change at another Chinese lab. This qualifies a literal same-experiment reading, but does not show that larger-model development had ceased.
Establishes a third Chinese company's relevant model program. A new model family alone does not establish repeated enlargement toward AGI.

payload.what_would_resolve: Obtain dated records for January 1 through November 27, 2025, with earlier models as comparison points. Support requires comparable size histories and explicit AGI links showing repeated enlargement as a central strategy at every named lab and at least three identified Chinese companies. Contradiction requires evidence that a named lab or a substantial part of the group did not pursue that strategy. Smaller releases or additional research methods alone would not settle it.

Ongoing-state claim with no named period. The target period is the half-year before the post, which covers the most recent major security studies published before it.

payload.rationale: The claim is read as saying that, as of the post on 11 February 2026, there were substantial documented doubts about the security of AI-generated code. The test period runs from 1 July 2025 to 11 February 2026. The claim is supported if credible studies from that period found substantial vulnerability rates in code written by LLMs or coding agents. On 30 July 2025, Veracode reported testing more than 100 LLMs on 80 curated coding tasks. The models introduced security vulnerabilities in 45% of cases. Veracode also said security performance had stayed unchanged over time (e1). A preprint first posted on 2 December 2025 tested coding agents on 200 real-world feature tasks. With SWE-Agent and Claude 4 Sonnet, 61% of solutions were functionally correct but only 10.5% were secure (e2). Both studies came out before the post and meet the support condition. The packet has no study from the period finding that AI-generated code was generally secure. A Veracode follow-up from 28 July 2026 reported a similar rate, but it came after the post and is context only (e3).
limitations: One main study comes from a security vendor with a commercial interest in highlighting risk. The other is a preprint.
Both studies use curated or selected test tasks, not audits of deployed AI-generated code.
'Very much in question' is qualitative. The evidence shows substantial documented doubt, not that all AI-generated code is insecure.
The article Marcus cites ('this article last week') was not identified.

evidence.excerpt: The study analyzed 80 curated coding tasks across more than 100 large language models (LLMs), revealing that while AI produces functional code, it introduces security vulnerabilities in 45 percent of cases.
evidence.explanation: A large test across more than 100 LLMs found vulnerabilities in 45% of cases. That is a substantial documented security problem in AI-generated code.

payload.rationale: The TechCrunch story Marcus cites exists. It is by Connie Loizos and was published on 9 February 2026 (e1). It describes in-progress UC Berkeley research at a 200-person tech company. In that research, an engineer said that with AI 'you don't work less. You just work the same amount or even more' (e1). The story also quotes a Hacker News commenter who said stress had tripled while productivity rose 'maybe 10%' (e2). The researchers link the extra work to 'fatigue, burnout' (e3). This meets the claim that some coders are starting to report burnout with modest gains. One caveat: the researchers say AI's boost to what workers can do is real (e3). The 'modest gains' part therefore rests mainly on the forum comment.
limitations: The evidence is a small set of reports: one interviewed engineer and one anonymous forum commenter. It does not show how common burnout is among coders.
The Berkeley study covers tech workers at one company, not only programmers, and the story does not quantify their gains.
The METR item on coding speed (e4) is dated after the post and serves only as context for 'wicked fast'.

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that GPT-4 has uneven abilities and can be depended on across only a small minority of relevant tasks.
The comparison concerns capable high-school students, not average adults or professional specialists.

I treat this as a snapshot immediately before publication. GPT-4 has no reporting quarter, so earlier evaluations are historical context rather than automatically decisive evidence of its June 2024 state.
Reliability means consistent successful performance across varied instances of a task. It does not require absolute infallibility.
criteria.support_condition: Representative evaluations of the relevant GPT-4 version and capable high-school students show both advantages and disadvantages, with dependable GPT-4 performance confined to a small minority of task categories.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative evaluations show dependable GPT-4 performance across a substantial breadth of relevant tasks, or otherwise disprove the asserted pattern of relative abilities.

payload.rationale: OpenAI’s March 2023 technical report reported human-level GPT-4 performance on the majority of the professional and academic exams it tested [e2]. Its March 14, 2023 disclosure acknowledged factual hallucinations and reasoning errors [e1]. These earlier findings establish reported strengths and limitations, but neither item measures GPT-4’s abilities against a matched group of capable high-school students or the proportion of tasks it performed reliably on June 5, 2024 [e1][e2]. They therefore leave the claim unresolved [e1][e2].
limitations: Both sources are company disclosures from 2023 and do not establish the performance of an identified June 2024 GPT-4 version [e1][e2].
Exam scores do not establish repeated success across a representative range of relevant tasks or a matched comparison with capable high-school students [e2].
Acknowledged factual and reasoning errors do not establish that only a small minority of task categories were reliable [e1].

evidence.explanation: OpenAI acknowledged factual and reasoning failures. This concerns the original release and does not establish that only a small minority of tasks were reliable in June 2024.

evidence.locator: Section 4, following Figure 4; Table 1 provides individual exam results
evidence.explanation: The report documents substantial exam performance, alongside weaker results on some exams. Exam scores neither establish consistent real-world success nor identify a representative population of smart high-school students.

payload.what_would_resolve: Representative evaluations of an identified GPT-4 version available on June 5, 2024, using a matched group of capable high-school students, disclosed prompting and tools, and repeated trials across defined task categories. A specified reliability threshold and task denominator would allow assessment of both relative abilities and the breadth of dependable performance.

our_interpretation: The claim concerns the spread of a view, not whether that view has been scientifically proved.
The plain reading is that skepticism about achieving reliable, broadly capable AI simply by adding training data had gained visible support among researchers and industry figures.
The comparison runs from 2022 through the January 9, 2025 post. This is a historical trend, rather than a financial-style observation requiring a latest reporting quarter.
Prevalence means broader public endorsement, not majority agreement. Marcus supplies no numerical threshold or population.

Statements about pretraining limits count when they question the sufficiency of that approach. Mere reports of slower improvements do not establish agreement with every part of Marcus's robustness hypothesis.
The reference to advocacy since 2022 is a historical component to verify, not a conditional forecast.
criteria.support_condition: Independent records confirm Marcus advanced the position in 2022, and contemporaneous reporting or public statements document a subsequent broadening of similar skepticism by January 9, 2025.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable historical records refute the advocacy timeline, or comparable evidence shows that endorsement of the view remained unchanged or declined. Continued disagreement alone would not contradict an increase in prevalence.

payload.rationale: Big Think's December 22, 2024 report confirms that Marcus argued in 2022 that deep learning faced limits in reasoning and reliability [e1]. In November 2024, Reuters reported prominent scientists questioning pretraining scaling, including Sutskever, and TIME described related skepticism as gaining ground [e2, e3]. These reports support a qualitative increase in public support for doubts about scaling alone before January 9, 2025 [e1, e2, e3]. Amodei continued to express confidence in scaling in November 2024, showing that the view remained disputed [e4].
limitations: The evidence does not measure prevalence in a defined population or establish majority agreement.
Doubts about pretraining limits do not establish endorsement of Marcus's precise robustness hypothesis or prove that hypothesis correct.
The Reuters article was accessed through an attributed reproduction.

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that contemporary LLM answers consistently sound appropriate to the task, while dependable answers are uncommon across ordinary uses.
Trustworthy means sufficiently correct and reliable for the task, rather than merely fluent. It does not require perfect performance on every conceivable question.
Superficial is assessed through the stated contrast between appropriate language and dependable answers, not as a separate claim about consciousness or internal understanding.

Because this is an ongoing state without a reporting interval, the target is the latest reportable snapshot immediately before publication, January 13, 2025. Earlier evaluations are context unless they establish that snapshot.
No numerical cutoff for 'rarely' is imposed; the evidence must establish that dependable answers are clearly uncommon or clearly common across a representative task mix.
criteria.support_condition: Representative evaluations of contemporary systems show consistently appropriate language but dependable answers only as an uncommon exception across ordinary tasks.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative evaluations show that dependable answers are common across ordinary tasks, or verified in-scope responses clearly fail the asserted invariant of task-appropriate language.

payload.rationale: The claim has an ordinary empirical reading, but the recovered evidence does not settle its breadth. Reliability research documents plausible errors and inconsistent behavior. A company coding evaluation also reports substantial success. Neither establishes how often ordinary contemporary answers were dependable, and neither tests invariant linguistic appropriateness across problems. Scoring the claim from selected failures or selected benchmark successes would impose a task distribution Marcus did not supply.
limitations: The cited evaluations predate the target snapshot and are context only.
Correct answers on selected tasks do not establish dependable behavior across uses.
The coding result is company-reported and involves tool-assisted work.
A numerical interpretation of rarity could change the assessment.

evidence.excerpt: However, larger and more instructable large language models may have become less reliable.
evidence.explanation: The abstract reports plausible wrong answers, difficulties supervising errors and remaining sensitivity to phrasing. Those findings inform the reliability concern, but do not establish that dependable answers were rare across ordinary January 2025 uses.

evidence.excerpt: In an internal agentic coding evaluation, Claude 3.5 Sonnet solved 64% of problems, outperforming Claude 3 Opus which solved 38%.
evidence.explanation: The company reports successful solutions on a majority of its selected coding problems. This weighs against treating successful answers as universally rare, but an internal, tool-assisted coding evaluation does not measure general trustworthiness or the January snapshot.

payload.what_would_resolve: Representative evaluations of systems available at publication, with separate ratings of task-appropriate language and dependable answers, repeated trials, and explicit coverage of ordinary uses.

statement.document_title: AGI will not happen in your lifetime. Or will it?

our_interpretation: Plain reading: ChatGPT as it existed at the time of the post was far less capable than human intelligence in many respects, and its answers were too unreliable to trust without checking.
The testable core is reliability: did ChatGPT often give confident but wrong answers in the period from its launch on 2022-11-30 to the post on 2023-01-22?
'Cannot at all be trusted' is read as 'cannot be relied on', not as 'never says anything true'. The speaker himself grants it has talents.
criteria.support_condition: Credible sources from that period, including OpenAI itself or independent evaluators, document that ChatGPT often produced plausible but incorrect answers, so its output could not be relied on.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evaluations from that period show ChatGPT's answers were reliably accurate, so users could reasonably trust them without checking.

payload.rationale: The contract reads the claim as saying that ChatGPT was far less capable than human intelligence in many ways, and that its answers could not be relied on without checking. It scores the reliability part. OpenAI's launch post of 2022-11-30 said ChatGPT 'sometimes writes plausible-sounding but incorrect or nonsensical answers' (e1). On 2022-12-05, The Register reported that Stack Overflow had banned ChatGPT answers. Stack Overflow said 'the average rate of getting correct answers from ChatGPT is too low' and that the answers often needed a detailed read by someone with subject knowledge (e2). Both sources fall within the target period of 2022-11-30 to 2023-01-22. Both meet the support condition that ChatGPT's output could not be relied on without checking. The packet lists no counterevidence. The 'far inferior intelligence' part is hedged with 'in many ways' and has no set measure, so this verdict does not rest on it.
limitations: The evidence does not measure the 'far inferior intelligence' part. Neither source compares ChatGPT's overall intelligence with human intelligence.
'Cannot at all be trusted' is read as 'cannot be relied on'. The evidence does not test a literal reading that none of ChatGPT's answers could be trusted.
Neither source gives a measured error rate. OpenAI says 'sometimes', and Stack Overflow says the rate of correct answers is 'too low'.
Stack Overflow's statement covers answers posted to its site, which were mostly about programming. It is quoted through a news report because the primary policy page could not be read.

evidence.excerpt: ChatGPT sometimes writes plausible-sounding but incorrect or nonsensical answers.
evidence.explanation: The developer itself said, at launch, that ChatGPT gives plausible but wrong answers. This supports the claim that its output could not be trusted without checking.

our_interpretation: 'Current' means agents as of the post date; I use 2025 up to 2025-08-03.
Plain reading of 'grossly vulnerable': in realistic tests, attackers can reliably make most frontier agents break their rules.

Plain reading of the cause: the attacks work because agents respond to surface features of input (injected text, fake system tags, fake reasoning) and do not grasp who is actually instructing them or what the task really requires. Evidence that agents cannot tell trusted from untrusted instructions counts toward this.
criteria.support_condition: Large-scale tests show most current agents can be made to violate policies with modest effort, and successful attacks exploit the agents' failure to tell genuine instructions from injected or spoofed text.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Tests show current agents resist most attacks, or the main attacks succeed through causes unrelated to how agents interpret instructions (for example, ordinary software bugs in the surrounding system).

payload.rationale: The vulnerability part is supported. Zou et al. posted a red-teaming study on 28 July 2025, before the post. It reports 1.8 million prompt-injection attacks on 22 frontier agents across 44 realistic deployment scenarios, and over 60,000 of them caused policy violations. On the study's benchmark of 19 models, nearly all agents violated policy for most behaviors within 10–100 queries (e1). On the cause, the study describes common successful attacks. Attackers inserted text that mimics the model's own reasoning, or fake system tags carrying new instructions (e2). In a 16 June 2025 post, Simon Willison writes that LLMs cannot reliably weigh instructions by where they came from, because all input ends up as one sequence of tokens (e3). The contract counts evidence that agents cannot tell trusted from untrusted instructions toward Marcus's causal claim. Both parts of the support condition are met. 'Superficial understanding' is Marcus's wording. The researchers describe the mechanism in other terms.
limitations: No study in the packet tests 'superficial understanding' as a cause directly. The causal link rests on how successful attacks worked and on one expert's explanation.
The causal reading depends on treating the inability to separate trusted from untrusted instructions as a form of superficial understanding.
The study used realistic deployment scenarios. The evidence does not show how often the same attacks succeed against deployed products.
Marcus's 1.45% figure for the most secure system was not checked.

evidence.explanation: Over 60,000 successful attacks across 22 frontier agents, and nearly all agents broke policy within 10–100 queries. That is gross vulnerability.

evidence.excerpt: This attack involves injecting text that mimics the model’s internal reasoning, often using tags like "<think>" or similar structures.
evidence.locator: section on attack strategies, Faux Reasoning (Attacker 2 in Figure 8)
evidence.explanation: Successful attacks work by imitating surface forms (fake system tags, fake reasoning) that fool agents about who is instructing them. This fits a shallow grasp of the request.

evidence.excerpt: LLMs are unable to reliably distinguish the importance of instructions based on where they came from.

evidence.explanation: A leading practitioner explains that agents are exploitable because they cannot tell the user's instructions from injected ones, which is a failure to understand what they are actually being asked.

our_interpretation: The claim is about LLM agents up to the post date; I use 2025 up to 2025-08-03.

our_interpretation: The ordinary reading of the final sentence concerns the direction of progress toward robust, trustworthy agents. It is stronger than saying agents had not yet achieved reliability.

Robust, trustworthy agents are read as agents that perform ordinary delegated tasks dependably, including under foreseeable variations and disruptions. This operational description is the evaluator's interpretation.
The necessity statement about robustness identifies the destination. It does not by itself establish the empirical assertion about LLM progress.

Because the statement describes an ongoing state without a reporting period, July 2025, the latest completed month before the post, is the assessment period. Earlier measurements can supply historical context for that trajectory.
The surrounding doubts about what LLMs will ever achieve do not turn this present-tense claim into a forecast with an invented deadline.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable evidence about the trajectory into July 2025 shows that successive LLM-based agents were not making meaningful, transferable progress toward dependable task completion and resilience to foreseeable disruptions. Merely documenting continued failures is insufficient.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable evidence about the trajectory into July 2025 shows meaningful, transferable improvements in dependable task completion and resilience across ordinary agent tasks. Reaching perfect reliability is unnecessary, but isolated capability gains do not alone establish this broader progress.

payload.rationale: The claim concerns progress toward trustworthy agents, not simply whether agents were already trustworthy. METR supplies material evidence of increasing task horizons. The user-coordination benchmark supplies evidence of continuing weaknesses, but those weaknesses do not establish a stalled trajectory. A later reliability study finds small improvements, yet its aggregate result does not settle the July 2025 observation. The reviewed evidence therefore establishes neither the broad lack of progress asserted nor a sufficiently broad contrary trajectory.
limitations: The reporting window and operational meaning of progress are evaluator interpretations.
Software task horizons, user coordination, and broad operational reliability measure different aspects of agent performance.
The available evidence does not justify treating benchmark gains as complete proof of trustworthy operation or persistent failures as proof of no progress.

evidence.excerpt: Furthermore, frontier AI time horizon has been doubling approximately every seven months since 2019, though the trend may have accelerated in 2024.
evidence.explanation: This is material counterevidence to a claim of no agent progress: the study measures longer tasks completed at a fixed success probability. Its March findings and software-focused task suite do not establish the broader July trajectory in trustworthy operation.

evidence.excerpt: In particular, our experiments show significant performance drops when agents shift from no-user to dual-control, highlighting the challenges of guiding users.
evidence.explanation: The experiments identify a relevant weakness in agents that must guide users. This comparison between operating conditions does not show whether successive LLM systems were advancing toward reliability.

evidence.excerpt: The rise of LLM-based agents has opened new frontiers in AI applications, yet evaluating these agents remains a complex and underdeveloped area.
evidence.publisher: Mahmoud Mohammadi and coauthors via arXiv
evidence.explanation: This contemporaneous survey identifies limitations in evaluating agents. It helps explain the measurement gap but supplies no outcome test of Marcus's trajectory claim.

evidence.excerpt: Evaluating 14 agentic models across two complementary benchmarks, we find that recent capability gains have only yielded small improvements in reliability.
evidence.publisher: Stephan Rabanser and coauthors via arXiv

payload.what_would_resolve: Comparable evaluations of successive LLM-based agents covering the trajectory into July 2025, with repeated ordinary tasks and foreseeable disruptions, could establish whether reliability improvements transferred across settings or consistently failed to do so.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: AI agents released or shown in 2025 would fail a large share of realistic multi-step tasks, falling well short of the near-perfect reliability needed to trust them without supervision.
Independent or academic benchmarks of realistic agent tasks published in 2025 are the right test. Top-agent success rates well below 90% on such tasks count as 'not all that reliable'.
This assessment does not test whether 'all we will have are demos'. It tests only the reliability part.
criteria.support_condition: Evaluations published in 2025 show leading agents failing a substantial share (for example, a third or more) of realistic multi-step tasks, or documented live deployments show frequent errors.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evaluations published in 2025 show leading agents completing realistic, varied multi-step tasks with high reliability (for example, above about 90%) across the board.

payload.rationale: In January 2025, Marcus forecast that the year's AI agent demos would not work very reliably. The 2025 horizon has passed. Under the contract, the claim is supported if 2025 evaluations show leading agents failing a substantial share of realistic multi-step tasks. A third or more is the contract's example. In the September 2025 revision of TheAgentCompany, the most competitive agent completed 30% of workplace tasks autonomously (e1). On CRMArena-Pro, published in May 2025, leading agents reached about 58% single-turn success and about 35% multi-turn success on business tasks (e2). On 29 September 2025, Anthropic reported that Claude Sonnet 4.5 led OSWorld, a computer-task benchmark, at 61.4% (e3). In the same release, Anthropic reported 77.2% on SWE-bench Verified, a coding benchmark, averaged over 10 trials (e4). Each of the first three results implies failure on more than a third of tasks, which meets the support condition. None of the four results reaches the contract's contradiction bar of about 90%.
limitations: 'Not all that reliably' has no numeric threshold. The outcome depends on the contract's example that failing a third or more of tasks counts as not reliable.
The evidence is mostly benchmark scores. It does not give failure rates for agents in real deployments.
Results vary by domain. The 77.2% coding score (e4) is well above the other results.
The OSWorld and SWE-bench figures (e3, e4) were reported by Anthropic, not by an independent party.
This assessment does not test the claim that 2025 would bring only demos.
OpenAI's Operator evaluation page could not be read (HTTP 403).

our_interpretation: Only the factual part is scored: that as of January 2025 no method existed that reliably and verifiably eliminated or solved hallucinations in generative AI / LLMs. The claim that reliable agents require solving hallucination is a premise about what agents need and is not scored.

Plain reading of 'principled trustworthy answer': a method, grounded in theory, that reliably prevents or removes hallucinations across general use, so that outputs can be trusted. Methods that only reduce hallucination rates, or detect some of them, do not count as such an answer.
Target period: January 2025, the month of the post. The post describes an ongoing state ('still no') without naming a period.

payload.rationale: On 15 January 2025, Marcus wrote that there was still no principled, trustworthy answer to AI hallucination. Only this factual part is scored. A Nature news feature published 21 January 2025 was headlined 'AI hallucinations can't be stopped — but these techniques can limit their damage'. Its standfirst said large language models were still struggling to tell the truth. A Georgia Tech summary of that feature said researchers were working to make hallucinations less frequent and less problematic. OpenAI's system card for o3-mini, a model dated 31 January 2025, reported a 14.8% hallucination rate on PersonQA. OpenAI wrote that more work was needed to understand hallucinations. A June 2024 Nature paper describes a statistics-grounded method that detects a subset of hallucinations, called confabulations. Detecting a subset does not meet the contract's test of a method that reliably prevents hallucinations in general use. None of the cited sources describes such a method.
limitations: 'Principled trustworthy answer' has no stated threshold. The assessment uses the contract's reading: a method that reliably prevents hallucinations in general use.
The body of the Nature feature was paywalled. The assessment relies on its headline, standfirst and a university summary.
No January 2025 snapshot of a hallucination leaderboard was found.
The semantic entropy paper dates from June 2024, before the target period, and is used only as context.
The view that reliable agents need hallucination solved is a premise and was not assessed.

Together these support the observable part of the claim for the September to December 2025 period. The stronger reading, that LLMs can never stop hallucinating, is not tested here. our_interpretation: The condition is that someone builds the comprehension challenge he describes: a well-funded ($25-50M scale) test where systems watch full TV shows or films and answer questions. The questions are refreshed to avoid contamination, answers are scored carefully (perhaps by hand), and the machine is kept on the same footing as a first-time human viewer.
'Current system' means AI systems available around the post date, 2025-04-02.
'Not come close' means a large gap between the best such system and human viewers.
criteria.support_condition: A test meeting the condition is built, and systems from around April 2025 score far below human viewers on it.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A test meeting the condition is built, and a system from around April 2025 scores at or near human level on it.

payload.rationale: The claim is conditional. If someone carefully builds the comprehension challenge Marcus described, no system available around April 2025 would come close to human performance. He gave no deadline. The contract scores the claim only after a test meeting his design conditions is published with human and April-2025-era system results. The evidence packet contains no such test as of 2026-10-28. The only evidence item is LVBench, a long-video benchmark paper available 2025-10-20 (e1). It reports human accuracy of 94.4% on average. Gemini-2.5-Pro scored 67.4% and Seed1.5-VL scored 64.0%. That gap points the same way as the claim. But LVBench uses multiple-choice questions. Per e1, it is not refreshed against contamination and lacks the other design features in his condition. So it does not meet the antecedent, and the forecast stays unresolved.
limitations: The evidence does not show that any test meeting the stated conditions exists: full shows, refreshed questions, careful scoring and secure first-time-viewer conditions.
LVBench results do not show how systems would perform on open-ended explanation questions.
The contract sets no numeric threshold for 'come close', so how a future result is read will depend on interpretation.
The search may have missed a recent or obscure implementation of the challenge.

evidence.explanation: A long-video benchmark shows a large human-model gap, which points the same way as the claim. But it is multiple-choice, is not refreshed against contamination, and lacks the other design features he set as the condition, so it does not trigger the condition.

from_speaker: AI can do at least some of the work that junior employees can do

our_interpretation: Plain reading: in 2025, AI systems could do a real share of workplace tasks, but often could not complete whole jobs or projects end to end, and often fell short of experienced professionals' quality or judgment.
The period is the state of AI around the post, read as calendar 2025. Capability tests of the models available then were published in September–October 2025.
criteria.support_condition: 2025 evaluations show AI matching humans on a meaningful share of tasks, while failing on many whole projects or falling short of experts on a large share of tasks.
criteria.contradiction_condition: 2025 evaluations show AI routinely completing whole junior roles end to end and matching senior professionals on nearly all tasks, or doing almost none of the work.

payload.rationale: The claim is read as a description of AI in calendar 2025. Two preprints published in October 2025 tested 2025 models, and both fit the claim. The Remote Labor Index (submitted 30 Oct 2025) tests AI agents on real-world projects to measure end-to-end performance. The best agent reached an automation rate of 2.5% (e1). So agents rarely completed whole projects. GDPval (submitted 5 Oct 2025) builds its tasks from the work of professionals with an average of 14 years' experience (e3). On its 220-task gold subset, 47.6% of deliverables from Claude Opus 4.1, the best model there, were graded as better than or as good as the human deliverable (e2). That is a real share of tasks at expert level, but it is not all of them. Neither study shows AI routinely completing whole jobs end to end, matching experts on nearly all tasks, or doing almost none of the work. Those are the contract's tests for contradiction.
limitations: The benchmarks measure tasks and projects, not junior or senior job titles. They do not measure judgement directly.
'Often' is not quantified. Whether a match rate near half counts as 'often lacks' is a matter of degree.

The GDPval text gives 47.6% for Claude Opus 4.1, but the same section also says model deliverables matched or beat experts in 'just over half' of tasks. The evidence does not settle which figure applies to which comparison.
Both studies came out after the post (23 Aug 2025), though they test models from 2025.
The result covers 2025 only. It says nothing about later models.

evidence.excerpt: AI agents perform near the floor on RLI, with the highest-performing agent achieving an automation rate of 2.5%.
evidence.publisher: Center for AI Safety and Scale AI (arXiv)
evidence.explanation: On real paid projects, 2025 frontier agents completed only about 2.5% end to end. AI often cannot do the whole job.

evidence.excerpt: 47.6% of deliverables by Claude Opus 4.1 were graded as better than (wins) or as good as (ties) the human deliverable.
evidence.explanation: The best 2025 model matched or beat professionals on about half of tasks. So AI can do some of the work, but it fell short of experienced humans on the rest.

evidence.excerpt: Tasks are constructed from the representative work of industry professionals with an average of 14 years of experience.
evidence.explanation: The GDPval comparison is with senior professionals, so it bears on the senior-judgment part of the claim.
